## Monte Albán and artisan villages: Oaxaca's history and living crafts

The area surrounding [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) offers much more than museums. Ancient archaeological sites stand alongside villages where artisans still carve wooden figures, paint them by hand, and make pottery using techniques passed down through families. The Ada Tours **Monte Albán, Alebrijes and Black Clay** excursion brings together three distinct stops in one day.

The itinerary includes [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/), [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/), and [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/). **The duration is 8 hours**, with a scheduled start between **9:00 and 9:30 a.m.** The excursion is offered in **English and Spanish**, with a certified bilingual guide.

This is a good choice for travelers who want to understand how Zapotec heritage relates to the region's culture today and see craftspeople at work, rather than only browsing finished souvenirs.

## Monte Albán: a ceremonial capital on a mountaintop

[Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/) is one of southern Mexico's most important archaeological sites. The ancient city stands on high ground overlooking the valleys of Oaxaca. Ceremonial plazas, stepped structures, ball courts, tombs, and fragments of carved stone reliefs have survived.

UNESCO recognizes **the Monte Albán archaeological site and Oaxaca's historic center** as a single World Heritage property. Its official description pays particular attention to how the ancient city's inhabitants reshaped the mountain slopes with terraces, platforms, and stone structures. Monte Albán played a major role in the history of the Zapotec people and other communities of the region.

During the visit, the guide explains the layout of the main plaza and the purposes of the surviving spaces. It is important to distinguish established archaeological evidence from attractive but unproven stories: not every stone structure has a precisely known ritual function.

The site is mostly open-air. Wear comfortable shoes and bring water and sun protection.

## San Antonio Arrazola: where alebrijes are made

The next stop is [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/), one of the villages known for producing **alebrijes**. These brightly colored fantastical creatures are carved from wood and covered in elaborate painted patterns.

The creative process is part of the attraction: an artisan selects a piece of wood, shapes a silhouette, and gradually adds colorful designs. Some figures combine features of several animals, making each piece different from the next.

At a workshop, visitors can see pieces at different stages and discuss techniques with the craftspeople. Buying a figure is entirely optional, and purchases are not included in the excursion package.

Arrazola's alebrijes belong to Oaxaca's modern craft tradition. They should not be presented as an unchanged art form from Monte Albán's era: this is a distinct, living craft with its own history of development.

## San Bartolo Coyotepec: the black clay tradition

[San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/) is famous for **barro negro**, or black pottery. At family workshops, visitors can watch clay being shaped, finished by hand, and polished, and see completed vessels.

The contrast between an ordinary raw material and the finished result is particularly striking. After processing, the ceramic surface may develop a deep dark color and a noticeable sheen. It is an excellent complement to Arrazola: in one village, artisans work with wood and color; in the other, with malleable clay and its surface.

Handle the pieces carefully and ask the artisans for permission before photographing their work. Buying souvenirs is not obligatory, and any purchases are personal expenses.

## What the eight-hour excursion includes

Our excursion includes the following:

| Included | Paid separately |
|---|---|
| Shared transport | Meals |
| Bilingual guide | Tips |
| Admission to Monte Albán | Personal purchases |
| Workshop visits | Personal expenses |

The planned start time is **9:00–9:30 a.m.**, and the duration is **8 hours**. The excursion operates in English and Spanish. A Russian-speaking guide is not listed as a standard service.

Admission to the archaeological zone is included. Purchases in the artisan villages, meals, and tips are paid for separately. The price of a standalone excursion must be agreed separately.

## Monte Albán or a walking tour of Oaxaca: which to choose?

If you have **a full day**, the Monte Albán itinerary with two villages combines archaeology and workshops. If you only have **half a day**, another option is a [walking tour of central Oaxaca](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/) featuring Santo Domingo Church and the main square.

These excursions complement each other. Monte Albán lies outside the city center, and the artisan villages require transfers; the city walk focuses on Oaxaca's architecture, streets, and cultural life. On a longer trip through [Mexico](/mexico/), they can be scheduled on separate days.

## Frequently asked questions about Monte Albán and alebrijes

### Can all three stops be visited in one day?

Yes. Ada Tours offers them together in one **8-hour** itinerary: Monte Albán, San Antonio Arrazola, and San Bartolo Coyotepec.

### Is admission to Monte Albán included?

Yes. The published list specifically includes **admission to Monte Albán**, shared transport, a bilingual guide, and workshop visits.

### Can I buy alebrijes and pottery?

Workshop visits are part of the itinerary, but any purchases are personal expenses. You are not required to buy anything.

### What language is the excursion conducted in?

**English and Spanish**. These are the confirmed languages of the published program; Russian interpretation is not included by default.

### Are the artisan villages part of the UNESCO property?

The UNESCO designation covers **Oaxaca's historic center and the archaeological zone of Monte Albán**. Visits to Arrazola and San Bartolo Coyotepec add an introduction to the region's contemporary craft traditions.

## Tours visiting Monte Albán and Oaxaca's artisan villages

[Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/) is an archaeological complex on high ground above the [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/) valley. Its broad plazas, temple platforms, and stone buildings preserve traces of one of pre-Columbian Mexico's great cultures. The Ada Tours excursion combines a visit to the site with two artisan villages: [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/) and [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/).

The excursion module takes about **8 hours**. However, you can choose tours of different lengths and onward routes: one focuses on Oaxaca, while the other crosses several regions of Mexico. It is therefore more useful to compare the full itineraries than just the name of the excursion.

| Tour | How the visit fits in |
|---|---|
| [Five days in Oaxaca](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) | Monte Albán and workshops on day 3 |
| [Viva Mexico, 12 days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) | The same excursion module on day 7 |

Both itineraries include the confirmed standalone [Monte Albán, Alebrijes and Black Pottery excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/). The trip's overall duration determines how much time you spend in other cities and whether you can stay in Oaxaca for additional cultural activities.

## Five days in Oaxaca: more time in one region

[Oaxaca: a 5-day short getaway](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) suits travelers interested in the urban culture and archaeology of southern Mexico. After arriving and checking into your hotel, you explore Oaxaca's historic center, then take an excursion to Monte Albán and the two artisan villages. The next day continues to Mitla, Teotitlán del Valle, and Hierve el Agua, including traditional weaving and other regional experiences.

This option avoids repeated journeys between distant regions of the country. All 4 nights are spent at a hotel in Oaxaca. Airport transfers are private on this itinerary, while the guided excursions and transport on days 2–4 are shared. The certified guide speaks English and Spanish.

The trip introduces several distinct craft traditions and goes beyond souvenir shopping. After seeing the painting of wooden figures and the firing of black pottery, you can compare them with Teotitlán's weaving. In this format, Monte Albán forms part of an in-depth introduction to Oaxaca.

## Twelve days through Mexico: Monte Albán on a longer journey

[Viva Mexico: Mexico City, Oaxaca and Yucatán in 12 days](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/) is designed for travelers seeking archaeology in several regions. Here Monte Albán is visited on **day 7**, after a walking tour of Oaxaca's historic center. Subsequent stages lead to other attractions in southern Mexico and on the Yucatán Peninsula.

Oaxaca occupies only part of this longer itinerary, making it a good option for a varied first visit to Mexico if you can set aside almost 2 weeks. Alongside Monte Albán, you will see other archaeological and cultural sites; the program also includes natural attractions and the [Santa Bárbara cenotes](/mexico/place/santa-barbara-cenotes/).

The 12-day tour includes shared transfers and excursions, accommodation in standard rooms with breakfast, admission to historical sites, and a bilingual guide. Domestic and international flights, additional meals, and personal expenses are excluded. Compare its cost with an Oaxaca-only trip in light of the flights and everything included in each itinerary.

## What you will see on the excursion

At Monte Albán, the focus is on Zapotec heritage. UNESCO recognizes the archaeological site and Oaxaca's historic center together as a World Heritage property. The main plaza is surrounded by stone platforms and the buildings of the ceremonial center; the guide explains how the complex was used, its inhabitants' worldview, and life in the ancient city.

The route then continues to [San Antonio Arrazola](/mexico/place/san-antonio-arrazola/). Local artisans carve fantastical figures from wood and decorate them with colorful painted designs. Watching the work is particularly engaging: how a piece is shaped, colors selected, and patterns created. Alebrijes are part of a modern Mexican craft tradition and should not automatically be described as ancient Zapotec archaeological artifacts.

The final stop is [San Bartolo Coyotepec](/mexico/place/san-bartolo-coyotepec/), known for black clay pottery. At a workshop, visitors may observe vessels being shaped, polished, and decorated. In this way, the archaeological day continues with the region's living crafts.

## Services included in the excursion module

The excursion lasts approximately 8 hours and begins between **9:00 and 9:30 a.m.** It includes shared transport, a certified English- and Spanish-speaking guide, admission to Monte Albán, and visits to artisan workshops. Meals, tips, and personal expenses are listed separately.

When choosing a full tour, focus on what is included in that particular multi-day program. An additional excursion or service within the 5- or 12-day journey does not automatically become private. Compare the guiding and transport arrangements for individual days.

If you would like just one day trip without a multi-day tour, see the [standalone Monte Albán and artisan villages excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/). For a broader choice of destinations, explore the [Mexico tours catalog](/mexico/tour/).

## Frequently asked questions about tours featuring Monte Albán

### Which Ada Tours tours include this excursion?

It features on day 3 of the [5-day Oaxaca getaway](/mexico/tour/oaxaca-city-break-5-days/) and day 7 of the [12-day Viva Mexico itinerary](/mexico/tour/viva-mexico/). Both use the same standalone excursion program.

### Which is better: 5 or 12 days?

If your main priority is Oaxaca's history, crafts, and culture, the 5-day option gives you more time in a single region. If you want to combine Monte Albán with other parts of Mexico, choose the 12-day itinerary.

### Are alebrijes and black pottery the same craft?

No. Arrazola's alebrijes are primarily brightly painted carved wooden figures. San Bartolo Coyotepec is known for distinctive methods of working and polishing black clay pottery. Both workshops are visited on the excursion.

### Can I expect a Russian-speaking guide?

The excursion module specifies English and Spanish. Russian-language guidance cannot be assumed to be included without separate agreement.

### Is lunch included in the eight-hour excursion?

The standalone excursion description lists meals among the exclusions. Multi-day tours have their own meal arrangements, which should be checked in the chosen itinerary.

## Excursions to the National Museum of Anthropology: choosing a Mexico City itinerary

The [National Museum of Anthropology](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/) introduces visitors to Mesoamerican civilizations and the cultures of Mexico's Indigenous peoples today. It can be incorporated into a journey through the capital in different ways: as part of an exploration of the historic center or after a visit to the city's main pilgrimage complex. The right choice depends on which context matters most to you.

We include the museum on **two different excursions**. One connects archaeology with the history of the city's buildings, while the other combines religious shrines with museum collections. Their schedules and places visited differ.

## The route with the Zócalo and Chapultepec

The [Mexico City: Zócalo, Chapultepec and Anthropology Museum excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/) starts in the historic center. The itinerary includes [Zócalo Square](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), the [Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), an introduction to the heritage of the [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/), and a journey along Paseo de la Reforma to [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/). The museum completes this historical sequence.

The museum portion introduces Mexica culture, the Sun Stone, Maya heritage, Olmec monuments, and material relating to Teotihuacán. The advantage is that the city's historic sites and the museum exhibits illuminate one another: first you see the site of ancient Tenochtitlán, then objects and evidence from its culture.

Access to the interior of the National Palace on the same excursion is possible **only when the building is open to visitors**. It should not be treated as a guaranteed part of the itinerary.

## The route with the Shrine of Guadalupe

The [Basilica of Guadalupe, Mass and Anthropology Museum excursion](/mexico/basilica-of-guadalupe/guadalupe-mass-anthropology/) is structured differently. It begins at the [Shrine of Guadalupe](/mexico/place/basilica-of-guadalupe/), visiting the Old and New Basilicas, chapels, and other parts of the complex, and attending Holy Mass. The museum visit follows the religious portion.

This option suits travelers whose journey is both a pilgrimage and a cultural or historical experience. It offers an opportunity to see contemporary Mexican religious traditions and the material heritage of earlier eras in a single day.

This excursion includes **private transport, an English-speaking guide, admission tickets to the listed attractions, and one Mass**. The conditions of this specific itinerary should not automatically be applied to other excursions in the catalog.

## How much museum time should you allow during a longer excursion?

The National Museum of Anthropology is very large, and trying to visit every gallery as part of a busy city itinerary is difficult. For a first visit, choose a few key collections. For example, you might focus on the Mexica hall and related historical subjects, then spend more time with Maya culture, the cultures of Oaxaca, or the ethnographic collections on another visit.

If the museum is your primary goal, confirm in advance how much time remains for the exhibits after transfers and other stops. A detailed guide to its galleries and layout appears on the museum's [own page](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/). Both established itineraries include other significant stops, so neither promises a complete tour of every collection.

## Practical considerations before visiting

The museum is near [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/). According to official INAH information, its usual visiting days are Tuesday through Sunday; check hours, prices, and access to specific collections again for your chosen date. With so much material to see, breaks and comfortable shoes are useful, and the order of excursions should take Mexico City's traffic into account.

## Frequently asked questions about excursions featuring the Anthropology Museum

### Can I combine the museum with Mexico City's historic center?

Yes. On the [Zócalo and Chapultepec excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/), the museum shares a day with the historic center and the park.

### Which option should I choose for a pilgrimage?

The [Shrine of Guadalupe itinerary](/mexico/basilica-of-guadalupe/guadalupe-mass-anthropology/) is appropriate: it includes Mass followed by a museum visit.

### Does either itinerary include every gallery in the museum?

Neither program makes that promise. The extent of the museum visit depends on the schedule, transfers, and selected exhibits. Mention any galleries of particular interest when booking.

## Excursions to Mexico City's National Palace: routes and visiting conditions

The [National Palace of Mexico City](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/) stands beside the [Zócalo](/mexico/place/mexico-city-zocalo/), the main square of the historic center. Its long façade and position near the cathedral help visitors understand the capital's layout, while the interior houses famous murals by Diego Rivera. When choosing an excursion, it is important to distinguish **viewing the palace from the square** from **entering the building**.

The palace remains an active government building. Its inclusion in an excursion therefore does not guarantee access to its courtyards, murals, or historic halls. Current registration procedures and restrictions need to be checked ahead of the visit.

## The historic center and Anthropology Museum

On the [Mexico City: Zócalo, Chapultepec and Anthropology Museum excursion](/mexico/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/mexico-city-zocalo-chapultepec-anthropology/), the National Palace forms part of a broader introduction to the capital. The route first crosses the Zócalo to the [Metropolitan Cathedral](/mexico/place/mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral/), then explores the history of the [Templo Mayor](/mexico/place/templo-mayor/), continuing to [Chapultepec](/mexico/place/chapultepec/) and the [National Museum of Anthropology](/mexico/place/national-museum-of-anthropology/).

This itinerary's advantage is a coherent introduction to Mexico City's history. You can connect the site of ancient Tenochtitlán, colonial architecture, modern government buildings, and museum collections. One restriction applies: **the National Palace can only be entered when visitor access is open**.

## A pilgrimage route through churches and squares

Another option is [Mexico City Churches, Mass and Garibaldi Square](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/). It starts in the historic center and includes Holy Mass at [Santo Domingo Church](/mexico/place/santo-domingo-mexico-city/), a visit to the cathedral, an introduction to the city's palaces, and a continuation to Garibaldi Square, famous for its mariachi music.

This is a separate **religious and cultural** program. It includes private transport, an English-speaking guide, admission to the listed accessible sites, and one Mass. The excursion conditions explicitly warn that visiting the National Palace depends on the current government schedule and may not be possible. Any time inside the building must be arranged for the specific day.

## What if the palace is closed?

Closed interiors do not prevent a walking tour of the Zócalo. From outside, you can see the façade and the palace's relationship to the surrounding landmarks. Nearby are the cathedral and the archaeological site of the Templo Mayor, both important to understanding the area's history.

If Diego Rivera's murals are your main priority, make this clear when choosing a route. According to official INAH information, some visits within the palace use advance registration, but separate procedures and restrictions apply. **Booking a general Mexico City excursion does not itself guarantee registration or admission.**

The building's history, mural subjects, and differences between possible visit routes are covered in detail on the [National Palace page](/mexico/place/national-palace-mexico-city/). Here you can choose a city itinerary and ask which attractions will be accessible.

## Choosing the right excursion

For a first visit to Mexico City spanning several eras of its history, the route through **the Zócalo, Chapultepec, and the Anthropology Museum** is a good fit. If the day's focus is **Mass and churches**, the itinerary featuring Santo Domingo and Garibaldi Square makes more sense. In both cases, the palace is one stop within a wider route, while entry to its interior requires separate confirmation.

## Frequently asked questions about National Palace excursions

### Can I be sure of seeing Diego Rivera's murals?

No. Access to the interior depends on administrative decisions and official events. This restriction needs to be considered when planning either excursion.

### Can I see the National Palace without going inside?

Yes. Its façade faces the Zócalo and can be viewed from outside on a tour of the historic center. This is not equivalent to visiting the halls.

### Which excursion includes Holy Mass?

Mass is part of the [pilgrimage route through Mexico City's churches](/mexico/santo-domingo-mexico-city/mexico-city-pilgrimage-garibaldi/). The excursion featuring the Zócalo and Anthropology Museum has a different itinerary.

## Excursions in Oaxaca: a city walk or a trip beyond the center

In [Oaxaca](/mexico/place/oaxaca/), you can devote half a day to the churches and squares of the historic center, or spend a full day exploring archaeological sites, craft workshops, and natural landmarks. We offer three separate excursions in and around the city, each with a different focus. First decide what you most want to see, then consider the duration.

The historic center of Oaxaca is a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the archaeological complex of Monte Albán. However, these sites are in different locations. An ordinary walking tour of the center does not include a trip to the pyramids.

## Three itineraries: how do they differ?

| Excursion | Main focus |
|---|---|
| [Oaxaca walking tour](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/) | 4 hours: Santo Domingo, tourist street, Zócalo |
| [Monte Albán and artisan villages](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/) | 8 hours: archaeology, alebrijes, black pottery |
| [Mitla and Hierve el Agua](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/) | 9–10 hours: ruins, weaving, nature, mezcal |

These are the lengths of three separate excursions. They are not a single mandatory package; specific dates and the order of visits can be discussed while planning your trip.

## The historic center: 4 hours for a first introduction

The [Oaxaca city sightseeing tour](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/) explores the historic center. The main architectural stop is Santo Domingo de Guzmán Church, known for its Baroque interior. The program continues with a walk along the Andador Turístico, with its artisan shops and galleries, and the main Zócalo square.

On this itinerary, the guide connects Oaxaca's colonial history with the pre-Hispanic heritage of the Zapotec and Mixtec peoples. It is a good first-day option: after the tour, there is time to return independently to a museum, gallery, or market you particularly enjoyed.

The excursion lasts **4 hours**, starts between **9:00 and 9:30 a.m.**, and is offered in English and Spanish. Shared transport, a certified bilingual guide, and admission to historic sites are included. Meals, tips, personal expenses, and tickets to optional attractions are paid for separately. A cooking workshop and mezcal tasting are mentioned as additional possibilities after the main walk, so they cannot be treated as part of the four-hour excursion.

## Monte Albán: archaeology and craftspeople at work

The [Monte Albán and artisan villages excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/) starts at the ancient ceremonial center on a hill overlooking the valley. Ball courts, temples, plazas, and other structures of the Zapotec city survive here. This is a different aspect of the region's heritage from Oaxaca's Spanish colonial street grid.

The route continues to San Antonio Arrazola, where visitors learn how brightly painted wooden alebrije figures are made, and to San Bartolo Coyotepec, known for its black clay pottery. Travelers see not just finished souvenirs but the work that goes into making them.

The program lasts **8 hours**, with a scheduled start from **9:00 to 9:30 a.m.** It includes shared transport, a bilingual guide, admission to Monte Albán, and workshop visits; meals and personal expenses are excluded. For a deeper introduction to the pre-Hispanic city, see the [Monte Albán](/mexico/place/monte-alban/) page.

## Mitla, weaving and natural landscapes

If you want to compare the valley's archaeological sites, choose the [excursion to Mitla and Hierve el Agua](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/). [Mitla](/mexico/place/mitla/) is known for its geometric stone mosaics, while [Hierve el Agua](/mexico/place/hierve-el-agua/) is famous for mineral formations resembling frozen waterfalls.

On the same day, the itinerary includes an introduction to weaving in Teotitlán del Valle and a visit to a mezcal producer with a tasting. It is a full **9–10-hour** excursion with varied stops, suited to travelers willing to spend almost the whole day outside the city. Shared transport, a certified bilingual guide, admission to the archaeological sites and Hierve el Agua, and the tasting are included. Meals, tips, and personal expenses are separate.

## How to divide your days in Oaxaca

If you have only one free half-day, the historic center is the most sensible choice. With a full day and a strong interest in ancient history, the trip to Monte Albán is a better fit. Travelers keen to combine archaeology, workshops, and unusual natural formations are likely to prefer the Mitla itinerary.

To take all three excursions, you will need separate time slots. Do not try to combine two- and three-hour stops from different itineraries into one day without allowing for driving time. Before choosing, review your actual arrival and departure schedule, the excursion language, and which optional visits you really want.

You can extend your plans through our [Mexico tour catalog](/mexico/tour/) or compare [cultural journeys across the country](/interests/culture-and-history/tours/mexico/).

## Frequently asked questions about Oaxaca excursions

### Can I see Monte Albán on the four-hour city walk?

No. The [city tour](/mexico/oaxaca/oaxaca-walking-tour/) focuses on the historic center. Monte Albán has its own [eight-hour excursion](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/).

### Are there Russian-language excursions in Oaxaca?

These three programs specify English and Spanish. Russian-speaking guidance is not confirmed and must be arranged separately before booking.

### Are mezcal tasting and workshop visits included in every excursion?

No. Mezcal tasting is included on the Mitla route, while the Monte Albán excursion includes artisan workshop visits. Cooking and tasting activities on the city walk are listed as optional extras.

### Which excursion is best for learning about Zapotec history?

For archaeological monuments, choose [Monte Albán](/mexico/monte-alban/monte-alban-craft-villages-tour/); to compare archaeological sites and stone ornamentation, explore [Mitla](/mexico/mitla/mitla-hierve-el-agua-mescal-tour/). Both differ from the walking tour of the colonial city.
